title: Module 0 · Hospital Pharmacy 101
intro: Start here if you have never worked in a hospital. How the queue, the chart, the MAR, the cabinets and the people fit together, and how to think through any order.

cases.title: Your first order in the queue
cases.setting: First shift · central pharmacy · verification queue
cases.stem: You log in and the first order is: **enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily** for a 78 year old woman admitted with pneumonia. It looks routine. Before you click verify, you need a system you run on every order, every time.

steps.q: What do you look at before you even read the drug?

options.t: The patient: name, age, weight, allergies (with the reaction), pregnancy or breastfeeding status
options.why: Every dose decision depends on who the patient is. A wrong weight or a missed allergy makes a correct looking order dangerous.

options.t: The price of the drug
options.why: Cost matters for formulary work, but it is not part of the safety check on a new order.

options.t: Which nurse is assigned
options.why: Useful later if you need to call, but it does not tell you if the order is safe.

options.t: Whether the prescriber is an attending or a resident
options.why: Every order gets the same check no matter who wrote it.

steps.teach: Build the habit: **patient first, then indication, then drug.** Experienced pharmacists check the same things in the same order so nothing gets skipped at 3 a.m.
steps.where: Weight, allergies and age are in the patient banner at the top of the chart in the EHR (St. Mary's uses Cerner, also called Oracle Health). If the weight says "stated" or is missing, ask the nurse for a measured weight.

steps.q: Why does the indication matter for enoxaparin?

options.t: The same drug has very different doses for prevention vs treatment of a clot
options.why: Enoxaparin 40 mg daily is a prophylaxis dose. Treatment is 1 mg/kg every 12 hours. If the patient actually has a clot, 40 mg daily is a big underdose.

options.t: It does not matter; 40 mg is the standard dose for everyone
options.why: 40 mg is standard only for medical prophylaxis with normal kidney function.

options.t: It changes which nurse gives it
options.why: Indication drives the dose, not the staffing.

steps.teach: If you cannot name why a drug is ordered, you cannot judge the dose. When the indication is missing, look at the problem list and admission note, then ask.

steps.q: Which lab do you need before you verify enoxaparin?

options.t: Serum creatinine, so you can estimate creatinine clearance
options.why: Enoxaparin is cleared by the kidneys. If CrCl is below 30 mL/min, prophylaxis drops to 30 mg daily (FDA label).

options.t: Hemoglobin A1c
options.why: Diabetes control does not change the enoxaparin dose.

options.t: Lipid panel
options.why: Not related to anticoagulant dosing.

options.t: Platelets
options.why: Low platelets raise bleeding risk and can be a clue to heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Check a baseline.

steps.teach: Renal function and platelets are the two labs to check on every anticoagulant. You will learn the Cockcroft Gault formula in the next case.
steps.where: Labs tab in the chart; look at the trend, not just today's number.

steps.q: Her CrCl is 62 mL/min, platelets 210, no clot, no epidural planned, no other anticoagulant. What do you do?

options.t: Verify the order as written
options.why: Indication, dose, kidney function and duplicates all check out.

options.t: Change it to 30 mg daily
options.why: The 30 mg dose is for CrCl below 30 mL/min.

options.t: Hold it until the team calls you
options.why: There is no problem to fix; holding delays clot prevention.

steps.teach: Verifying is also a decision. When everything checks out, verify and move on, so you have time for the orders that need you.

cases.monitor: Platelets and hemoglobin periodically, kidney function as it changes, signs of bleeding.
cases.pearl: **Patient, indication, labs, drug, duplicates, then decide.** Same order, every time.

sources.t: FDA label, Lovenox (Sanofi)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Calculating creatinine clearance
cases.stem: An order needs a renal dose check. Patient: 70 year old man, 80 kg (measured), height 5 ft 10 in, serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL.

steps.q: Which formula do most drug labels use for renal dose adjustments?

options.t: Cockcroft Gault creatinine clearance
options.why: Most label renal dosing tables were built using Cockcroft Gault, so it is the usual formula for drug dosing.

options.t: Body mass index
options.why: BMI describes weight for height, not kidney function.

options.t: The anion gap
options.why: That is an acid base calculation.

steps.teach: CrCl (mL/min) = [(140 minus age) x weight in kg] / (72 x SCr), times 0.85 for females.

steps.q: Calculate his CrCl with actual body weight.

options.t: About 49 mL/min
About 69 mL/min
options.why: Check the denominator: 72 x 1.6, not 72 alone with rounding.

options.t: About 41 mL/min
options.why: That would be the female value (x 0.85). He is male.

options.t: About 122 mL/min
options.why: That skips the creatinine in the denominator.

steps.teach: Write it out every time on paper or in the calculator. Rounding early causes errors.

steps.q: When should you stop and think about which weight to use?

options.t: When the patient is obese, very thin, or the weight looks wrong for the height
options.why: Weight choice (actual, ideal or adjusted) changes the result a lot. Follow St. Mary's policy for which weight to use.

options.t: Never; always use actual weight
options.why: In obesity, actual weight can overestimate clearance.

options.t: Only for children
options.why: Weight choice matters in adults too.

steps.teach: Also be careful when creatinine is changing fast (acute kidney injury). A single value can make CrCl look better than it is.
steps.where: St. Mary's renal dosing policy and the pharmacy dosing guide (verify which weight they use).

cases.pearl: **(140 minus age) x kg over 72 x SCr, times 0.85 if female.** Recheck weight choice in obesity.

sources.t: Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Prediction of creatinine clearance from serum creatinine. Nephron 1976;16:31-41
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Missing allergy reaction
cases.stem: A patient has "penicillin" on the allergy list with no reaction listed. Cefazolin is ordered for cellulitis.

steps.q: What is your first move?

options.t: Find out what the reaction actually was
options.why: A childhood rash is very different from anaphylaxis. The reaction decides what is safe.

options.t: Reject cefazolin because the patient is allergic to penicillin
options.why: Cefazolin has a different side chain and very low cross reactivity. Rejecting it may push the team to a worse drug.

options.t: Verify without looking further
options.why: Allergy checks are part of every antibiotic order.

steps.teach: "Allergy" lists are often wrong or vague. Clarifying them is one of the highest value things a pharmacist does.
steps.where: Ask the patient or nurse: what happened, how soon after the dose, how was it treated, and have they taken a penicillin or cephalosporin since? Check prior encounters in the chart.

steps.q: The patient says: "I got an itchy rash as a kid. I had cephalexin last year with no problem." What now?

options.t: Verify cefazolin and update the allergy entry with the reaction and the tolerated cephalosporin
options.why: Low risk history plus a tolerated cephalosporin. Documenting the details helps every future pharmacist.

options.t: Ask for a vancomycin order instead
options.why: Vancomycin is less effective for typical cellulitis and has more toxicity.

options.t: Hold until an allergist sees the patient
options.why: Not needed for a low risk history.

steps.teach: Your documentation outlives your shift. Write the reaction, the date and what was tolerated.

cases.pearl: **Every allergy gets a reaction.** No reaction listed means you ask.

sources.t: Brameli, Stone, Phillips. J Allergy Clin Immunol Glob 2024 (cites 2022 drug allergy practice parameter)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Who do I call?
cases.stem: At 1 a.m. you find a vancomycin order that is double the dose you expect. You need to change it.

steps.q: Who can change the order?

options.t: The prescriber (or the covering prescriber at night)
options.why: Only a prescriber can change the order, unless a pharmacy protocol lets you adjust it (for example a pharmacy to dose vancomycin policy).

options.t: The patient's nurse
options.why: The nurse is your partner and a great source of information, but cannot change the order.

options.t: The pharmacy technician
options.why: Technicians support you but do not change orders.

steps.teach: At night the daytime prescriber is usually not the one to call. Find out who is covering (night float, hospitalist, on call resident).
steps.where: The chart's care team list, the unit secretary, or the paging directory. Ask the nurse, "Who is covering tonight?"

steps.q: Does St. Mary's let pharmacists adjust vancomycin without calling?

options.t: Check the policy: many hospitals have a pharmacy to dose protocol
options.why: If a protocol covers it, you may adjust and document. If not, you call.

options.t: Yes, always, at every hospital
options.why: Authority depends on each hospital's protocols.

options.t: No, never
options.why: Many hospitals do allow pharmacy dosing for vancomycin and aminoglycosides.

steps.where: Pharmacy policies on the St. Mary's intranet; ask your manager or a senior pharmacist on your first week.

steps.q: The prescriber says, "Just verify it," and you still believe it is unsafe. What next?

options.t: Explain the risk once more with your source, then follow the chain of command if you still disagree
options.why: Most hospitals have an escalation path: senior pharmacist or pharmacy supervisor, then the attending or medical director. Never verify an order you believe will harm the patient.

options.t: Verify it; the prescriber is responsible
options.why: You are responsible for what you verify.

options.t: Delete the order
options.why: You cannot remove a prescriber's order on your own.

steps.teach: Escalating is not confrontation. Say: "I'm not comfortable verifying this dose because [reason, source]. I'm going to involve my supervisor so we can settle it quickly."
steps.where: Chain of command policy (verify locally). Write down names, times and what was said.

cases.call: **S:** This is [name], the pharmacist, calling about [patient] in [room]. **B:** Vancomycin 2,500 mg every 12 hours is ordered; weight 70 kg, creatinine 1.4. **A:** That is about double the usual dose for this weight and kidney function, which raises the risk of kidney injury. **R:** I recommend [dose] and a level [when]. Can I change it?
cases.pearl: **Prescriber changes orders. Nurse gives information. Supervisor helps when you disagree.**

sources.t: IHI: SBAR toolkit
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: The MAR
cases.stem: A nurse calls: "Did the patient get the 0600 antibiotic? The day nurse isn't sure."

steps.q: Where do you look?

options.t: The MAR (medication administration record)
options.why: The MAR shows what was scheduled, what was given, when, and by whom, plus doses held or refused.

options.t: The order itself
options.why: An order shows what should be given, not what was given.

options.t: The pharmacy dispensing log
options.why: Dispensed does not mean administered.

steps.teach: Learn the difference: **ordered** (order), **dispensed** (pharmacy or cabinet), **given** (MAR). Errors live in the gaps between them.
steps.where: MAR tab in the chart. Look for "given," "not given," "held" and the reason.

steps.q: The MAR shows the dose as "not given, patient off unit." What matters most now?

options.t: Getting the dose given as soon as possible and adjusting the next dose time if needed
options.why: For time sensitive drugs like antibiotics, a missed dose matters. Work out the timing with the nurse.

options.t: Writing an incident report before anything else
options.why: Reporting may be right later, but the patient comes first.

options.t: Nothing, the next dose is fine
options.why: Skipping antibiotic doses can lead to treatment failure.

sources.t: St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: The automated dispensing cabinet override
cases.stem: An ED nurse removed a drug from the automated dispensing cabinet (often called Pyxis or Omnicell) on override before you verified the order.

steps.q: When is a cabinet override appropriate?

options.t: Emergencies where waiting for pharmacist review would harm the patient, using drugs on the approved override list
options.why: Override exists for urgent situations. The list of drugs allowed on override is set by policy.

options.t: Any time the nurse is busy
options.why: Convenience overrides skip the pharmacist safety check.

options.t: Never
options.why: Codes and true emergencies need fast access.

steps.teach: The Joint Commission expects hospitals to have policies for dispensing cabinets and to review overrides.
steps.where: St. Mary's automated dispensing cabinet policy and override list (verify locally).

steps.q: What is your job after an override?

options.t: Review the order as soon as possible as if it had not been given yet, and follow up if there is a problem
options.why: Retrospective review still catches errors, and the next doses depend on your review.

options.t: Nothing, the drug was already given
options.why: Later doses and monitoring still need your review.

cases.pearl: **Override is for emergencies. You still review it.**

sources.t: Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Five pages at once
cases.stem: At 2 a.m. these all arrive in the same 5 minutes: (1) a code blue page, (2) a nurse asking if a tablet can be crushed, (3) a STAT tenecteplase request for a stroke alert, (4) a routine antibiotic order, (5) a question about a drug interaction for a discharge tomorrow.

steps.q: Which do you handle first?

options.t: The code and the stroke alert, at the same time if needed (call for backup)
options.why: Both are life threatening and time critical. Codes and stroke alerts come before everything else. If you are alone, ask the nurse supervisor or a second pharmacist for help.

options.t: The routine antibiotic, because it was first in the queue
options.why: First in is not most urgent.

options.t: The discharge question, because it is easy
options.why: Easy is not urgent.

steps.teach: Sort by **harm if delayed**: life threatening now, then time sensitive (first antibiotic doses, STAT orders), then routine, then questions for later.
steps.where: St. Mary's code and stroke alert response policies tell you which pharmacist responds (verify locally).

steps.q: After the emergencies, what is next?

options.t: The new antibiotic order (time sensitive first dose)
options.why: First doses of antibiotics are time sensitive, especially in sepsis.

options.t: The discharge interaction question
options.why: That can wait until morning or later in the shift.

steps.q: The crush question: how do you answer it fast and correctly?

options.t: Check the ISMP Do Not Crush list and the product (extended release, enteric coated)
options.why: Crushing extended release products can dump a full day's dose at once.

options.t: Tell the nurse it is always fine to crush
options.why: Many products cannot be crushed.

steps.where: ISMP Do Not Crush list, the drug label, or Lexicomp through St. Mary's.

cases.pearl: **Life threatening, then time sensitive, then routine, then questions.**

sources.t: ISMP: High alert medications in acute care settings
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Answering a drug information question
cases.stem: A nurse asks: "Can I give this IV drug through the same line as the heparin drip?"

steps.q: What do you ask before you answer?

options.t: Which drug, what concentration, and what else is running in that line
options.why: Compatibility depends on the exact drugs and concentrations. Background questions turn a vague question into an answerable one.

options.t: Nothing, just say yes
options.why: Guessing causes precipitates and blocked lines.

options.t: The nurse's years of experience
options.why: Not relevant to compatibility.

steps.teach: Systematic approach: get the background, figure out the real question, search, answer clearly, and document.

steps.q: Where do you look for Y site compatibility?

options.t: A compatibility reference such as Trissel's or King Guide (through St. Mary's), or the free Stabilis site
options.why: These list drug pairs tested together.

options.t: A general search engine
options.why: Results are unreliable for compatibility.

options.t: The drug's marketing website
options.why: Not a compatibility reference.

steps.where: See your IV Compatibility page in the Drug Hub for the classic ones.

steps.q: You cannot find data for this pair. What do you tell the nurse?

options.t: No data means do not run them together; use a separate line or flush between
options.why: Absence of data is not proof of safety.

options.t: It is probably fine
options.why: "Probably" is not an answer for an IV line.

sources.t: ASHP guidelines on the pharmacist's role in providing drug information

cases.title: High alert drug double check
cases.stem: An insulin infusion is ordered. It is on the ISMP high alert list.

steps.q: What does "high alert" mean?

options.t: Errors with these drugs are more likely to cause serious harm
options.why: High alert drugs are not always used wrongly more often, but when an error happens the harm is bigger (ISMP).

options.t: They are used more often than other drugs
options.why: Frequency is not the definition.

options.t: They are more expensive
options.why: Not related.

steps.q: Which safeguards help most with high alert infusions?

options.t: Standard concentrations matched to the smart pump library
options.why: Removes math and custom mixing errors.

options.t: Independent double checks where policy requires them
options.why: A second person checks independently, not by just looking over the first person's shoulder.

options.t: Premixed bags when available
options.why: Fewer manipulations, fewer errors.

options.t: Writing "be careful" on the label
options.why: Warnings without a system change rarely prevent errors.

cases.pearl: **High alert = high harm when wrong.** Standardize, use the pump library, double check.

sources.t: ISMP: High alert medications in acute care settings

cases.title: Do Not Use abbreviations
cases.stem: An order reads: "Insulin regular 10U IV x1" and another reads "Morphine 2.0 mg IV q4h PRN."

steps.q: What is wrong with these orders?

options.t: "U" can be misread as 0 or 4; write "units"
options.why: 10U can become 100.

options.t: A trailing zero (2.0 mg) can be misread as 20 mg
options.why: Write 2 mg.

options.t: Nothing; these are standard
options.why: Both are on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list.

steps.q: What should you write for a dose under 1 mg?

options.t: A leading zero: 0.5 mg
options.why: .5 mg can be misread as 5 mg.

options.t: .5 mg
options.why: Missing leading zero is a Do Not Use item.

cases.pearl: **No U, no IU, no trailing zero, always a leading zero.**

sources.t: Joint Commission Do Not Use list (Becker's summary)

cases.title: Reporting a near miss
cases.stem: You caught a 10 fold heparin error before it reached the patient.

steps.q: Should you report it?

options.t: Yes, report near misses through St. Mary's reporting system
options.why: Near misses show where the system is weak before someone is hurt.

options.t: No, nothing happened
options.why: The next time it may not be caught.

options.t: Only if the prescriber agrees
options.why: Reporting does not need permission.

steps.teach: In a just culture, human error gets support, at risk behavior gets coaching, and reckless behavior gets action. Reports fix systems, not people.
steps.where: St. Mary's event reporting system (verify the name and how to access it). ISMP also accepts voluntary reports.

cases.pearl: **Report near misses. They are free lessons.**

sources.t: ISMP
St. Mary's policies and order sets (verify locally)

cases.title: Shift handoff
cases.stem: You are leaving at 7 a.m. You are waiting on a vancomycin level, and a prescriber promised to call back about a duplicate order.

steps.q: What goes in your handoff?

options.t: Pending issues, who you are waiting on, what you recommended, and what to do if the callback does not come
options.why: The next pharmacist should be able to finish your work without starting over.

options.t: Only finished work
options.why: Finished work is already documented; pending items get lost.

options.t: Nothing; they will see it in the queue
options.why: Pending callbacks are not visible in the queue.

cases.pearl: **Hand off what is pending, not what is done.**

sources.t: IHI: SBAR toolkit

cases.title: Home medication reconciliation
cases.stem: A new admission lists "metoprolol, a water pill, and something for sugar." The team wants an accurate home list.

steps.q: Which sources make the home list accurate?

options.t: The patient or family, using open questions ("What do you take for your heart?")
options.why: Start with the person, then confirm.

options.t: Outpatient pharmacy fill history or a call to their pharmacy
options.why: Shows what was actually filled, with strength and directions.

options.t: Pill bottles brought from home
options.why: Confirms product and strength.

options.t: Guessing the usual dose
options.why: Guessing creates errors that follow the patient home.

steps.q: Why does it matter in the hospital?

options.t: Missed home drugs (for example a beta blocker) can cause withdrawal, and wrong doses carry into the discharge list
options.why: Errors at admission often become errors at discharge.

options.t: It only matters for billing
options.why: It is a safety process.

cases.pearl: **Ask the person, check the pharmacy, see the bottles.**

sources.t: Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)

cases.title: A drug is on shortage
cases.stem: The supplier says a drug you use often is on shortage.

steps.q: Where do you look for alternatives and the plan?

options.t: ASHP Drug Shortages for status and alternatives, plus St. Mary's written substitution protocol
options.why: The Joint Commission expects hospitals to have shortage plans and substitution protocols.

options.t: Tell prescribers to use whatever they like
options.why: Uncoordinated substitutions cause dosing errors.

steps.where: ASHP Drug Shortages (ashp.org/drug-shortages), St. Mary's pharmacy leadership and P&T announcements.

cases.pearl: **Shortage = status check, approved substitute, clear communication.**

sources.t: ASHP Drug Shortages
Joint Commission National Performance Goals 2026 (LAMMICO summary)
